extracted.intended_audience: prospective contestants, fans, journalists, and researchers interested in Britain's Got Talent format and rules
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the show's format, eligibility, audition and live-round rules, voting/advancement mechanisms, and production requirements as described on the Wikipedia page for Britain's Got Talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility / application information
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant that seeks to enter that year's competition must first submit an application to the programme, containing information about who is performing – whether a single person, a pair or trio of performers, and a small or large group – personal details regarding age, hometown and background, what experience they have for their talent, and the nature of the act that will be performed. Eligibility for the contest is determined by what information is submitted for researchers to double-check, such information is required, per the programme's terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications are checked by researchers and eligibility is determined based on submitted information; contestants of any age can audition (though practice and debate over children participating has occurred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open auditions (first round) format
rubrics_metrics.description: The first round, referred to as 'open auditions', are held across several different cities around the UK during the Autumn months, within small venues that are attended by the producers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open auditions are local, held near contestants' residences to allow access; additional open audition formats (e.g., YouTube submissions, in-store 'Talent Spot' events) have been used in some series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' Auditions (second round) format and venue setup
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judges' Auditions are held within theatres or convention halls chosen primarily for having the necessary facilities for handling large volumes of contestants. The venue is arranged into three zones consisting of a waiting area for participants, the wings where they enter and leave, and the main stage area that they perform on. These auditions are attended by the judges along with an audience who secure tickets to attend these sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production chooses venues with backstage/waiting facilities and audience seating; the session is staged for TV (audience present) and filmed for later editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audition performance time limit and backing track policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Once brought onto the main stage, they begin by engaging with the judges ... – whereupon they are given three minutes to conduct their performance. A backing track for their act is allowed if required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contestants should prepare a routine that fits within a three-minute audition slot; backing tracks are permitted when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' buzzers and termination of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A performance ends when either the time is up, or all the judges use their buzzers. Each judge has one [buzzer] ... to signal their dislike of the performance if they believe it to be unconvincing, boring or completely unacceptable for the contest (although a buzzer can be retracted if the judge felt they used it mistakenly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buzzers are used to signal disapproval and can in combination stop an audition; judges may later retract a buzzer if they change their mind due to unexpected elements in the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges' immediate feedback and voting at auditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a performance is over, each judge will give an overview of what they thought about the act, before casting a vote. If the contestant(s) receives a majority vote of 'Yes', they then proceed onto the next stage in the contest, otherwise they are eliminated at that point from the competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges provide verbal feedback then vote; majority 'Yes' required to advance from the Judges' Auditions to the next stage (subject to later deliberation rounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Buzzer automatic advancement (auditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning with the eighth series, judges can also grant an automatic place in the live rounds through the use of the 'Golden Buzzer' situated on their panel's desk ... which can be used by any of the judges for a participant whose audition was exceptional in their opinion, regardless of the views of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally constrained in usage per series (page records rules such as 'It may only be used twice by each judge' and hosts could press once), but practice/precedent (e.g., Bruno pressing twice) and later series' changes mean exact limits have varied; Golden Buzzer sends an act straight to live rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation Day / Judges' decisions process
rubrics_metrics.description: This stage (also referred to as Deliberation Day) is when the judges look through the acts that have successfully made it to this stage, and begin whittling them down to those who would stand a fair chance in the live semi-finals. The amount that goes through has varied over the show's history, though usually consists of a number that can be divided equally over the semi-finals being held in a series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges review successful auditionees and select a set number to progress to semi-finals; selection is based on perceived chances in live rounds rather than solely on audition pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-final performance requirements and live production safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Contestants who make it into the semi-finals ... must perform before the audience and judges, as well as on live television. As with the audition stage, each semi-finalist must conduct a performance before the judges – a new routine of their act – with the judges' role being to watch what is conducted and give feedback towards the end of the performance. Because all semi-finalists are performing live, they are given time to prepare in advance with rehearsals, while production staff can provide assistance. In the case of those conducting routines that incorporate a level of risk, precautions are put in place, including paramedics and sometimes set up off-site venues for performances to use – either live or for a pre-recorded film for the episode's live broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semi-final acts should be new routines, rehearse beforehand, and if risky, coordinate with production about safety measures and possible pre-recording or off-site setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-final advancement: public vote and judges' vote
rubrics_metrics.description: Each semi-final can only have two participants advance into the final, and these are determined by two votes. The first is public phone-in vote ... the semi-finalist with the highest total of votes is announced as the winner of the semi-final and secures their place in the final. The second vote involves the judges and takes place after the result, in which they vote between the two semi-finalists placed 2nd and 3rd respectively in the public vote, with the participant receiving the majority vote securing their place in the finals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advancement from each semi-final is a two-step process: top public vote winner advances automatically; judges choose between public 2nd and 3rd to determine the second qualifier. Procedures have varied by series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semi-final tie-breaker rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a tied [judges'] vote, as of series 5, the semi-finalist placed 2nd in the public vote advances into the final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If judges' decision ties, public vote placement (2nd) is used as tie-breaker; note that the show's rules on voting procedures have changed across series (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wildcard mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-finalists can also secure a place in the finals if chosen as a 'Wildcard'. Introduced in the sixth series, the format allows the judges to choose any eliminated semi-finalist to be appointed as their Wildcard in the finals, through a private vote conducted once the semi-finals are completed. The format was later expanded to allow for a Wildcard to be chosen by the public from any eliminated semi-finalist they liked in the ninth and tenth series respectively, though this format was dropped before the eleventh series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wildcards have been selected by judges or by public vote depending on series; availability and selection mechanism have changed historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finals: voting emphasis and announcement procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: The finals operate in a similar manner to the semi-finals, though all participants in this stage compete primarily to win votes from the public with either a new routine, or on some occasions, an enhanced version of their original audition performance. The judges can still buzz and give opinions on the performance they view, but have little impact on the public's voting intention. Once the public vote has been completed ... the hosts announce who is placed as the top two acts of the vote, before revealing the winner who received the most votes from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finals are primarily public-vote driven; judges' commentary is largely advisory. Public votes determine the top two and the eventual winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variations in advancement rules across series
rubrics_metrics.description: Format changes across series: e.g., for the eleventh series the Judges' vote was dropped with the two semi-finalists with the highest number of public votes moving on into the final; following criticism the judges' vote was reinstated in later series. From Series 18 the golden buzzer was added to the semi-finals, with one judge awarding a golden buzzer in each show sending an act straight through to the final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers have modified voting/advancement mechanisms across series; contestants and observers should check the current series' rules as they may differ from past practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public voting mechanisms (phone-in, app, website)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first [semi-final] vote is public phone-in vote (via a special phone-number) ... The show has also experimented with a mobile app for voting (a new voting method was trialled and in 2015 free in-app voting was introduced). As of 11 April 2022, the app is no longer available. Voting is now conducted through the ITV website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public voting technology and allowance (e.g., free app votes, phone-in) have changed over time; voting windows are timed during live broadcasts and votes are verified and counted before results announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filming, editing and selection for broadcast (highlighting notable auditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filming for each series begins during the Judges' Auditions, and always consists of recording taken from each venue of auditions and backstage scenes within the wings and waiting area. Footage taken by production staff is then edited into a series of episodes consisting of montages of scenes from multiple venues, consisting of the most notable auditions (the best, worst and funniest made) – along with interviews with some of the notable participants that auditioned, and recorded backstage scenes of the hosts overseeing the performances from the wings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all audition performances are broadcast; producers edit for narrative and entertainment, emphasizing particularly memorable, exceptional or viral moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of ID sticker requirement (contestant identification change)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Series 8 onwards, alongside the introduction of the 'Golden Buzzer', contestants are no longer required to wear an ID sticker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification/production procedures may change between series; contestants should follow current production instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling norms for live episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: For the show's scheduling, the live episodes are usually arranged to take place over the course of a week, semi-finals for each weekday, and the live final aired on either the Saturday or Sunday of the weekend. Exceptions have occurred (e.g., series where semi-finals were pre-recorded and weekly due to COVID-19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live scheduling is typically compact over a week but producers have adapted schedules due to external events (sporting broadcasts, pandemics); contestants should expect possible changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and pre-recording options for risky acts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of those conducting routines that incorporate a level of risk, precautions are put in place, including paramedics and sometimes set up off-site venues for performances to use – either live or for a pre-recorded film for the episode's live broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts involving physical risk must liaise with production safety teams; some dangerous routines may be pre-recorded or staged off-site rather than performed live on the main stage.
